Land Bank Liquidations: Victims & Vultures

By: Anina Peens | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Why were scores of commercial farmers liquidated by the Land Bank between 2018 and 2022?

Unique Selling Point:
The Land Bank of South Africa has launched a forensic investigation into its own internal legal team for allegedly conspiring with private lawyers to recklessly liquidate tens of commercial farmers across South Africa.



Summary:
The South African Landbank wants white commercial farmers off their land...or that is the narrative that has been created after scored of farmers lost their farms and business as a result of unpaid debt to the bank. However, the majority of the farmers' assets outweighed their debt and liquidation was thus a last resort. It seems that a corporate syndicate operated here, acting in their own financial interests and manipulating the liquidation ACT to push farmers of their land without giving them a chance for business rescue.

Further information:
It is just after 5am and already nearly 40 degrees Celsius. The sun is beaming down on the small town of Zeerust, in the Northwest Province of South Africa. Like every morning, for the last twenty-five years, Cois Harman has been waking up at the break of dawn to open the dairy. He loves the milkery, just as he loves the Swiss cattle breed, Braunvieh. In 2014 the agricultural research council presented Cois a platinum award for his outstanding breeding techniques of Braunvieh female animals.
That was when he still owned his own stud. That was when he still owned his own farms. It has been a long journey to come to accept his fate, make peace with his losses and move on to live a peaceful life. But the “vultures” are making sure, that doesn’t happen.
Cois lives off the profit he makes from his daily milk sales. And after a day of driving up and down the dusty roads, he returns home, to a portion of an old house in town, that belongs to his son. Because he does not even own a house anymore, the vultures took it all, he says. The biggest challenge to date was to accept that he can never return to his farm.

In his younger years, Cois Harman was a teacher. He wrote 4 different Setswana handbooks for the department of education, some that are still being used in schools today. He banked every cent he made off selling the handbooks until he had enough saved up to buy his first farm. He shows us where the land stretches across the wild bushveld planes, that he used to walk, nurture, and cherish. While he lived here, he also became the host of a radio show on Motsweding FM. For 13 years he would go on to host an agricultural talk show which he presented in Setswana to train small and upcoming farmers across South Africa. When the talk show ended, the training continued via several WhatsApp groups connecting farmers and serving as a training platform for farmers across the country, up until this very day. This is the closest he gets to his former life as farmer.

Seventy-two-year-old Cois is a victim of a system, far greater than himself. A system to which he is just a faceless insolvent.

In 2008, the Landbank entered into a service level agreement with UNIGRO, the financial arm of the agricultural cooperative, AFGRI. For generations, the cooperative established relationships with farmers in every province of the country. The agents knew the farmers and vice versa. The Landbank does not have a direct relationship with farmers as is the case with the cooperatives that mostly have offices or depots in most farming districts. And so, Landbank mandated UNIGRO to control its debtor’s book. The bank, established in 1912, has a mandate to avail finance to farmers to grow and expand the Agri sector, ensuring food security. The 2010 decision for Unigrow to expand on Landbank’s debt book included a renumeration of 180 million Rand annually. The interest on the debt was divided between Unigrow and Landbank. In other words, only the portion of the interest on the debt was paid to Land bank while UNIGRO essentially took the largest piece of the cake. For every loan that was furnished, agents received commissions. Land bank thus, made little money while UNIGROW was making a killing. Reckless lending was at the order of the day and some farmers admitted -off record- those large loans were made with little paperwork but approved by a handshake and motivated by good standing relationships between agents and farmers.
Over a period of 13 years, UNIGRO grew Land bank’s debtor book to 13 billion Rand.

But something strange started to happen in 2018. And only in 2022, did all the pieces of the puzzle start falling in place.
Cois Harman had two farms in the Groot Marico bushveld, valued at 6 million Rand, and paid in full. He applied for a loan of two million Rand from UNIGRO to acquire a third farm. He also applied and was granted a production loan to plant maize. By the time the maize was to be harvested, it would have been able to service the mortgage of new land. Cois’s debt was just over 4 million, and assets exceeded his debt. He was also an estate agent and thus had other sources of income and was waiting for funds to be released that would have put him in a position, coinciding with the expected harvest, to pay his debt in full. He made small payments (R50 000 and R250 000 when he was able to) on the debt and sent Unigro a letter with proof of his lawyer’s trust account in which money was deposited for a farm that he sold at the time. He had to wait for the transfer. He asked Unigrow for extension on his debt. Two Unigro agents visited him on the farm and agreed that he could get an extension of three months. They told him to sign a contract to commit to the extension and undertaking to pay the debt in full before the three-month extension lapsed.

But enter Henk Strydom. A lawyer from Pretoria, specializing in liquidation. Mandated by Unigro to assist in collecting outstanding debt from farmers, he is referred to as a ‘vulture, a money maniac and a cold-hearted reaper of land’, by many a farmer. Cois was served a summons and at the same time, a liquidation application process was started. Unigrow knew this when they visited Cois on his farm and the contract that Cois actually signed, was an acknowledgement that his farming business would be liquidated. Then began the most daunting five years of his life. No business rescue, restructuring of debt or any other solution he brought to the table, was considered and the legal fees from Henk’s office, started piling up.

It would only emerge much later, that more than 60 farmers experienced the same fate at the hands of Henk Strydom.

Jaco du Toit used to be a large commercial farmer from Koedoeskop, Thabazimbi. He had 12 fully functional companies that were all linked to each other. Topping this, he had 36 planes and helicopters he used in agriculture flying training programs. Jaco had good standing with all the cooperatives in his area. For 20 years he bought seed from Pioneer and paid in advance at the start of every new year. But the 2018 drought hit hard, and cash flow was a challenge. He was granted a 5.6 million Rand loan from Pioneer for seed for the year, loaned against his asset base of 380 million. When Jaco failed to pay an installment on the loan, he was summons and a liquidation application was made simultaneously against one of his businesses, Big Creek trading.
At this stage, Jaco had wheat on the land and the potential yield was estimated at 25 million Rand. Pioneer brought the liquidation application and Unigro seized the harvest.
Jaco now, could not access the wheat land as the land was hired from Big Creek against which the application was lodged. If he could harvest what was ready on the land, he would have been able to pay his entire debt to Pioneer.
After discussions with Nedbank, a restructuring of Jaco’s companies was on the table. Correspondence between Nedbank and Henk Strydom indicates that the bank was willing to take over the debt and restructure Jaco’s business. But, in a letter from Henk to the bank, Henk clearly states that he had orders from his client, the Land bank, to liquidate Big Creek. He was not open to any suggested rescue remedies.
Meanwhile, UNIGROW instructed Jaco to harvest the wheat, although legally, that is not permitted.
Jaco and his staff commenced with the harvest. As soon as Jaco moved the first load to storage, Henk brought a case of theft and contempt of court against Jaco. The paperwork started piling up and eventually Jaco would lose the fight because he could not afford the legal costs.
Over the next three years, Jaco’s entire farming operation was liquidated for less than 40% of his total asset value. His asset value was 380 million and his overall debt of all his businesses combined, amounted to just under 180 million Rand.

Meanwhile, Cois, who was still fighting to keep his assets, continued to try and find avenues to save what he had left. Out of frustration, he took to Facebook and publicized what he deemed to be unethical practice by Henk Strydom. Immediately, Henk hit back with a defamation case against Cois. Cois was instructed not to say anything on social media and was not allowed to mention Henk’s name. At the time, Cois had an operation on his back and was bedridden…A good place to contemplate what had happened to him. He made another post on Facebook but not mentioning Henk’s name. It was met with hundreds of replies from people who had experienced the same fate at the hands of Henk Strydom. After the follow up post was made, a police squad surrounded Cois’s home accompanied by two lawyers from Henk’s office in Pretoria. Cois was arrested and thrown in jail.

Back in Thabazimbi, it was a normal working day for employees at the Koedoeskop service station and restaurant. Another business belonging to Jaco but unrelated to Big Creek. Suddenly, Henk Strydom arrived on the premises, accompanied by a security firm. He ordered all employees to seize what they were doing and closed the shop and filling station. Restaurant patrons were told to leave the premises and employees ordered to cash up and leave. The business was shutting down. In 17 affidavits, employees echo the fear and anxiety they felt that day. Later that same day, there was a break-in at the premises and all CCTV cameras were stolen. A day later, they were returned by the same security team that accompanied Henk the previous day. All visual material had been deleted.

This conduct seems to be a pattern. Photos have now emerged of Henk and his friends, hunting on farms he was busy liquidating.

The Land bank terminated its service level agreement with UNIGRO in October 2021. An insider source within the Land bank cited the decision taken by the board to end the agreement, based on various discrepancies.
In a letter to their clients, dated October 2021, UNIGRO announced that the service level agreement between themselves and the bank was heading to an end. In the same letter, the cooperative confirms that the termination talks already started in March 2020. UNIGRO clients were advised to pay their Land bank debt straight to the Land bank. Another insider source within Henk’s personal circle told us, when Land Bank announced the termination of the SLA, Henk immediately applied for more than 40 liquidations in one go. Some of them are still ongoing. The bank and Unigro should reveal this. How many liquidation applications were brought between March 2020 and October 2021?

More than 60 farmers have the same story to tell; Of a systemic operation within the legal fraternity involved.
Connected between Henk Strydom, UNIGRO lawyer, Ernst Janse van Rensburg, the same set of liquidators, the same auctioneers, and a possible connection inside the Land Bank. I am in the process of getting my hands on documentation that may reveal fake creditors that were listed when payouts were made after liquidations concluded.

Up to date, no copy has been seen of Land Bank’s mandate to Henk Strydom. I would also like to see the correspondence in which the Land Bank refused Nedbank’s solution to save Jaco du Toit’s Big Creek.

The only documentation we have seen, is a power of attorney, given directly to Henk by Stephen Seboeng, Land Bank head of legal.
Seboeng joined the bank in 2018. (The first liquidations started in 2018). According to the Land bank insider, a legal panel of the bank jointly decides on a consultant if and when the bank intends to liquidate a debtor. There was seemingly never any decision taken by the bank to mandate Henk to act as liquidator. The only said power of attorney was granted in the Mafikeng high court between Stephan and Henk. Does the Land Bank have a paper trail reflecting this and how the decision was made to mandate Henk? To add insult to injury, the only existing power of attorney is dated October 2022. Other documentation reflecting Unigro’s mandate to take legal action against debtors, is a power of attorney signed by a regional manager of the Land Bank and four financial agents of Unigro: Ernst Janse van Rensburg is one of them. We know that Ernst and Henk are friends, golf and hunting buddies- but unfortunately, I cannot prove that, except to ask them. Unigro is protecting Ernst. I also know that Ernst was looking for another job mid last year, but I cannot prove that either.

The question remains, did the Land bank ever mandate Henk Strydom to liquidate farmers? In the long-term interest of national food security, was the bank aware that farmers were forced off their land and that this resulted in a general perception that the bank wanted white farmers off the land? Is there any truth in that? Liquidation should be the last resort when debt collection fails, according to industry experts. Should the farmers not have been offered restructuring? business rescue? How is it possible that the bank could give Strydom an order to liquidate Jaco’s Big Creek, if Nedbank was willing to take over the debt?

Cois Harman has lost everything. He should be entering into rehabilitation now that the liquidation and sequestration have concluded. But the defamation suits continue, and Henk slammed Cois with a legal bill of 1.3 million Rand in October 2021. According to Cois’s lawyers, Henk is now targeting Cois’s son to recover the money. Meanwhile, du Toit, the once commercial farmer, who created employment for over 600 people, are now living in a garden cottage of someone’s backyard. He had lost all he had left because the legal fees that came from Henk’s office never stopped.

On 11 May 2021, Schindlers attorneys and notaries lodged a complaint against Henk Strydom for misconduct and numerous contraventions of the code of conduct, to the South African legal counsel. They were Du Toit’s lawyers at the time. This, is apparently one of many complaints lodged by lawyers against Henk’s conduct that is widely described as unethical and inhumane. The firm asked for an investigation into Strydom’s firm, Strydom/Bredenkamp.

Unique Selling Point: The Land Bank of South Africa has launched a forensic investigation into its own internal legal team for allegedly conspiring with private lawyers to recklessly liquidate tens of commercial farmers across South Africa. Summary: The South African Landbank wants white commercial farmers off their land...or that is the narrative that has been created after scored of farmers lost their farms and business as a result of unpaid debt to the bank. However, the majority of the farmers' assets outweighed their debt and liquidation was thus a last resort. It seems that a corporate syndicate operated here, acting in their own financial interests and manipulating the liquidation ACT to push farmers of their land without giving them a chance for business rescue. Further information: It is just after 5am and already nearly 40 degrees Celsius. The sun is beaming down on the small town of Zeerust, in the Northwest Province of South Africa. Like every morning, for the last twenty-five years, Cois Harman has been waking up at the break of dawn to open the dairy. He loves the milkery, just as he loves the Swiss cattle breed, Braunvieh. In 2014 the agricultural research council presented Cois a platinum award for his outstanding breeding techniques of Braunvieh female animals. That was when he still owned his own stud. That was when he still owned his own farms. It has been a long journey to come to accept his fate, make peace with his losses and move on to live a peaceful life. But the “vultures” are making sure, that doesn’t happen. Cois lives off the profit he makes from his daily milk sales. And after a day of driving up and down the dusty roads, he returns home, to a portion of an old house in town, that belongs to his son. Because he does not even own a house anymore, the vultures took it all, he says. The biggest challenge to date was to accept that he can never return to his farm. In his younger years, Cois Harman was a teacher. He wrote 4 different Setswana handbooks for the department of education, some that are still being used in schools today. He banked every cent he made off selling the handbooks until he had enough saved up to buy his first farm. He shows us where the land stretches across the wild bushveld planes, that he used to walk, nurture, and cherish. While he lived here, he also became the host of a radio show on Motsweding FM. For 13 years he would go on to host an agricultural talk show which he presented in Setswana to train small and upcoming farmers across South Africa. When the talk show ended, the training continued via several WhatsApp groups connecting farmers and serving as a training platform for farmers across the country, up until this very day. This is the closest he gets to his former life as farmer. Seventy-two-year-old Cois is a victim of a system, far greater than himself. A system to which he is just a faceless insolvent. In 2008, the Landbank entered into a service level agreement with UNIGRO, the financial arm of the agricultural cooperative, AFGRI. For generations, the cooperative established relationships with farmers in every province of the country. The agents knew the farmers and vice versa. The Landbank does not have a direct relationship with farmers as is the case with the cooperatives that mostly have offices or depots in most farming districts. And so, Landbank mandated UNIGRO to control its debtor’s book. The bank, established in 1912, has a mandate to avail finance to farmers to grow and expand the Agri sector, ensuring food security. The 2010 decision for Unigrow to expand on Landbank’s debt book included a renumeration of 180 million Rand annually. The interest on the debt was divided between Unigrow and Landbank. In other words, only the portion of the interest on the debt was paid to Land bank while UNIGRO essentially took the largest piece of the cake. For every loan that was furnished, agents received commissions. Land bank thus, made little money while UNIGROW was making a killing. Reckless lending was at the order of the day and some farmers admitted -off record- those large loans were made with little paperwork but approved by a handshake and motivated by good standing relationships between agents and farmers. Over a period of 13 years, UNIGRO grew Land bank’s debtor book to 13 billion Rand. But something strange started to happen in 2018. And only in 2022, did all the pieces of the puzzle start falling in place. Cois Harman had two farms in the Groot Marico bushveld, valued at 6 million Rand, and paid in full. He applied for a loan of two million Rand from UNIGRO to acquire a third farm. He also applied and was granted a production loan to plant maize. By the time the maize was to be harvested, it would have been able to service the mortgage of new land. Cois’s debt was just over 4 million, and assets exceeded his debt. He was also an estate agent and thus had other sources of income and was waiting for funds to be released that would have put him in a position, coinciding with the expected harvest, to pay his debt in full. He made small payments (R50 000 and R250 000 when he was able to) on the debt and sent Unigro a letter with proof of his lawyer’s trust account in which money was deposited for a farm that he sold at the time. He had to wait for the transfer. He asked Unigrow for extension on his debt. Two Unigro agents visited him on the farm and agreed that he could get an extension of three months. They told him to sign a contract to commit to the extension and undertaking to pay the debt in full before the three-month extension lapsed. But enter Henk Strydom. A lawyer from Pretoria, specializing in liquidation. Mandated by Unigro to assist in collecting outstanding debt from farmers, he is referred to as a ‘vulture, a money maniac and a cold-hearted reaper of land’, by many a farmer. Cois was served a summons and at the same time, a liquidation application process was started. Unigrow knew this when they visited Cois on his farm and the contract that Cois actually signed, was an acknowledgement that his farming business would be liquidated. Then began the most daunting five years of his life. No business rescue, restructuring of debt or any other solution he brought to the table, was considered and the legal fees from Henk’s office, started piling up. It would only emerge much later, that more than 60 farmers experienced the same fate at the hands of Henk Strydom. Jaco du Toit used to be a large commercial farmer from Koedoeskop, Thabazimbi. He had 12 fully functional companies that were all linked to each other. Topping this, he had 36 planes and helicopters he used in agriculture flying training programs. Jaco had good standing with all the cooperatives in his area. For 20 years he bought seed from Pioneer and paid in advance at the start of every new year. But the 2018 drought hit hard, and cash flow was a challenge. He was granted a 5.6 million Rand loan from Pioneer for seed for the year, loaned against his asset base of 380 million. When Jaco failed to pay an installment on the loan, he was summons and a liquidation application was made simultaneously against one of his businesses, Big Creek trading. At this stage, Jaco had wheat on the land and the potential yield was estimated at 25 million Rand. Pioneer brought the liquidation application and Unigro seized the harvest. Jaco now, could not access the wheat land as the land was hired from Big Creek against which the application was lodged. If he could harvest what was ready on the land, he would have been able to pay his entire debt to Pioneer. After discussions with Nedbank, a restructuring of Jaco’s companies was on the table. Correspondence between Nedbank and Henk Strydom indicates that the bank was willing to take over the debt and restructure Jaco’s business. But, in a letter from Henk to the bank, Henk clearly states that he had orders from his client, the Land bank, to liquidate Big Creek. He was not open to any suggested rescue remedies. Meanwhile, UNIGROW instructed Jaco to harvest the wheat, although legally, that is not permitted. Jaco and his staff commenced with the harvest. As soon as Jaco moved the first load to storage, Henk brought a case of theft and contempt of court against Jaco. The paperwork started piling up and eventually Jaco would lose the fight because he could not afford the legal costs. Over the next three years, Jaco’s entire farming operation was liquidated for less than 40% of his total asset value. His asset value was 380 million and his overall debt of all his businesses combined, amounted to just under 180 million Rand. Meanwhile, Cois, who was still fighting to keep his assets, continued to try and find avenues to save what he had left. Out of frustration, he took to Facebook and publicized what he deemed to be unethical practice by Henk Strydom. Immediately, Henk hit back with a defamation case against Cois. Cois was instructed not to say anything on social media and was not allowed to mention Henk’s name. At the time, Cois had an operation on his back and was bedridden…A good place to contemplate what had happened to him. He made another post on Facebook but not mentioning Henk’s name. It was met with hundreds of replies from people who had experienced the same fate at the hands of Henk Strydom. After the follow up post was made, a police squad surrounded Cois’s home accompanied by two lawyers from Henk’s office in Pretoria. Cois was arrested and thrown in jail. Back in Thabazimbi, it was a normal working day for employees at the Koedoeskop service station and restaurant. Another business belonging to Jaco but unrelated to Big Creek. Suddenly, Henk Strydom arrived on the premises, accompanied by a security firm. He ordered all employees to seize what they were doing and closed the shop and filling station. Restaurant patrons were told to leave the premises and employees ordered to cash up and leave. The business was shutting down. In 17 affidavits, employees echo the fear and anxiety they felt that day. Later that same day, there was a break-in at the premises and all CCTV cameras were stolen. A day later, they were returned by the same security team that accompanied Henk the previous day. All visual material had been deleted. This conduct seems to be a pattern. Photos have now emerged of Henk and his friends, hunting on farms he was busy liquidating. The Land bank terminated its service level agreement with UNIGRO in October 2021. An insider source within the Land bank cited the decision taken by the board to end the agreement, based on various discrepancies. In a letter to their clients, dated October 2021, UNIGRO announced that the service level agreement between themselves and the bank was heading to an end. In the same letter, the cooperative confirms that the termination talks already started in March 2020. UNIGRO clients were advised to pay their Land bank debt straight to the Land bank. Another insider source within Henk’s personal circle told us, when Land Bank announced the termination of the SLA, Henk immediately applied for more than 40 liquidations in one go. Some of them are still ongoing. The bank and Unigro should reveal this. How many liquidation applications were brought between March 2020 and October 2021? More than 60 farmers have the same story to tell; Of a systemic operation within the legal fraternity involved. Connected between Henk Strydom, UNIGRO lawyer, Ernst Janse van Rensburg, the same set of liquidators, the same auctioneers, and a possible connection inside the Land Bank. I am in the process of getting my hands on documentation that may reveal fake creditors that were listed when payouts were made after liquidations concluded. Up to date, no copy has been seen of Land Bank’s mandate to Henk Strydom. I would also like to see the correspondence in which the Land Bank refused Nedbank’s solution to save Jaco du Toit’s Big Creek. The only documentation we have seen, is a power of attorney, given directly to Henk by Stephen Seboeng, Land Bank head of legal. Seboeng joined the bank in 2018. (The first liquidations started in 2018). According to the Land bank insider, a legal panel of the bank jointly decides on a consultant if and when the bank intends to liquidate a debtor. There was seemingly never any decision taken by the bank to mandate Henk to act as liquidator. The only said power of attorney was granted in the Mafikeng high court between Stephan and Henk. Does the Land Bank have a paper trail reflecting this and how the decision was made to mandate Henk? To add insult to injury, the only existing power of attorney is dated October 2022. Other documentation reflecting Unigro’s mandate to take legal action against debtors, is a power of attorney signed by a regional manager of the Land Bank and four financial agents of Unigro: Ernst Janse van Rensburg is one of them. We know that Ernst and Henk are friends, golf and hunting buddies- but unfortunately, I cannot prove that, except to ask them. Unigro is protecting Ernst. I also know that Ernst was looking for another job mid last year, but I cannot prove that either. The question remains, did the Land bank ever mandate Henk Strydom to liquidate farmers? In the long-term interest of national food security, was the bank aware that farmers were forced off their land and that this resulted in a general perception that the bank wanted white farmers off the land? Is there any truth in that? Liquidation should be the last resort when debt collection fails, according to industry experts. Should the farmers not have been offered restructuring? business rescue? How is it possible that the bank could give Strydom an order to liquidate Jaco’s Big Creek, if Nedbank was willing to take over the debt? Cois Harman has lost everything. He should be entering into rehabilitation now that the liquidation and sequestration have concluded. But the defamation suits continue, and Henk slammed Cois with a legal bill of 1.3 million Rand in October 2021. According to Cois’s lawyers, Henk is now targeting Cois’s son to recover the money. Meanwhile, du Toit, the once commercial farmer, who created employment for over 600 people, are now living in a garden cottage of someone’s backyard. He had lost all he had left because the legal fees that came from Henk’s office never stopped. On 11 May 2021, Schindlers attorneys and notaries lodged a complaint against Henk Strydom for misconduct and numerous contraventions of the code of conduct, to the South African legal counsel. They were Du Toit’s lawyers at the time. This, is apparently one of many complaints lodged by lawyers against Henk’s conduct that is widely described as unethical and inhumane. The firm asked for an investigation into Strydom’s firm, Strydom/Bredenkamp. Extra Budget Items: This shoot must happen in three different locations: Zeerust, Thabazimbi and Pretoria. I therefore request to film three days. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Why were scores of commercial farmers liquidated by the Land Bank between 2018 and 2022?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Land Bank of South Africa has launched a forensic investigation into its own internal legal team for allegedly conspiring with private lawyers to recklessly liquidate tens of commercial farmers across South Africa.
metadata.Summary: The South African Landbank wants white commercial farmers off their land...or that is the narrative that has been created after scored of farmers lost their farms and business as a result of unpaid debt to the bank. However, the majority of the farmers' assets outweighed their debt and liquidation was thus a last resort. It seems that a corporate syndicate operated here, acting in their own financial interests and manipulating the liquidation ACT to push farmers of their land without giving them a chance for business rescue.
metadata.Further information: It is just after 5am and already nearly 40 degrees Celsius. The sun is beaming down on the small town of Zeerust, in the Northwest Province of South Africa. Like every morning, for the last twenty-five years, Cois Harman has been waking up at the break of dawn to open the dairy. He loves the milkery, just as he loves the Swiss cattle breed, Braunvieh. In 2014 the agricultural research council presented Cois a platinum award for his outstanding breeding techniques of Braunvieh female animals. That was when he still owned his own stud. That was when he still owned his own farms. It has been a long journey to come to accept his fate, make peace with his losses and move on to live a peaceful life. But the “vultures” are making sure, that doesn’t happen. Cois lives off the profit he makes from his daily milk sales. And after a day of driving up and down the dusty roads, he returns home, to a portion of an old house in town, that belongs to his son. Because he does not even own a house anymore, the vultures took it all, he says. The biggest challenge to date was to accept that he can never return to his farm. In his younger years, Cois Harman was a teacher. He wrote 4 different Setswana handbooks for the department of education, some that are still being used in schools today. He banked every cent he made off selling the handbooks until he had enough saved up to buy his first farm. He shows us where the land stretches across the wild bushveld planes, that he used to walk, nurture, and cherish. While he lived here, he also became the host of a radio show on Motsweding FM. For 13 years he would go on to host an agricultural talk show which he presented in Setswana to train small and upcoming farmers across South Africa. When the talk show ended, the training continued via several WhatsApp groups connecting farmers and serving as a training platform for farmers across the country, up until this very day. This is the closest he gets to his former life as farmer. Seventy-two-year-old Cois is a victim of a system, far greater than himself. A system to which he is just a faceless insolvent. In 2008, the Landbank entered into a service level agreement with UNIGRO, the financial arm of the agricultural cooperative, AFGRI. For generations, the cooperative established relationships with farmers in every province of the country. The agents knew the farmers and vice versa. The Landbank does not have a direct relationship with farmers as is the case with the cooperatives that mostly have offices or depots in most farming districts. And so, Landbank mandated UNIGRO to control its debtor’s book. The bank, established in 1912, has a mandate to avail finance to farmers to grow and expand the Agri sector, ensuring food security. The 2010 decision for Unigrow to expand on Landbank’s debt book included a renumeration of 180 million Rand annually. The interest on the debt was divided between Unigrow and Landbank. In other words, only the portion of the interest on the debt was paid to Land bank while UNIGRO essentially took the largest piece of the cake. For every loan that was furnished, agents received commissions. Land bank thus, made little money while UNIGROW was making a killing. Reckless lending was at the order of the day and some farmers admitted -off record- those large loans were made with little paperwork but approved by a handshake and motivated by good standing relationships between agents and farmers. Over a period of 13 years, UNIGRO grew Land bank’s debtor book to 13 billion Rand. But something strange started to happen in 2018. And only in 2022, did all the pieces of the puzzle start falling in place. Cois Harman had two farms in the Groot Marico bushveld, valued at 6 million Rand, and paid in full. He applied for a loan of two million Rand from UNIGRO to acquire a third farm. He also applied and was granted a production loan to plant maize. By the time the maize was to be harvested, it would have been able to service the mortgage of new land. Cois’s debt was just over 4 million, and assets exceeded his debt. He was also an estate agent and thus had other sources of income and was waiting for funds to be released that would have put him in a position, coinciding with the expected harvest, to pay his debt in full. He made small payments (R50 000 and R250 000 when he was able to) on the debt and sent Unigro a letter with proof of his lawyer’s trust account in which money was deposited for a farm that he sold at the time. He had to wait for the transfer. He asked Unigrow for extension on his debt. Two Unigro agents visited him on the farm and agreed that he could get an extension of three months. They told him to sign a contract to commit to the extension and undertaking to pay the debt in full before the three-month extension lapsed. But enter Henk Strydom. A lawyer from Pretoria, specializing in liquidation. Mandated by Unigro to assist in collecting outstanding debt from farmers, he is referred to as a ‘vulture, a money maniac and a cold-hearted reaper of land’, by many a farmer. Cois was served a summons and at the same time, a liquidation application process was started. Unigrow knew this when they visited Cois on his farm and the contract that Cois actually signed, was an acknowledgement that his farming business would be liquidated. Then began the most daunting five years of his life. No business rescue, restructuring of debt or any other solution he brought to the table, was considered and the legal fees from Henk’s office, started piling up. It would only emerge much later, that more than 60 farmers experienced the same fate at the hands of Henk Strydom. Jaco du Toit used to be a large commercial farmer from Koedoeskop, Thabazimbi. He had 12 fully functional companies that were all linked to each other. Topping this, he had 36 planes and helicopters he used in agriculture flying training programs. Jaco had good standing with all the cooperatives in his area. For 20 years he bought seed from Pioneer and paid in advance at the start of every new year. But the 2018 drought hit hard, and cash flow was a challenge. He was granted a 5.6 million Rand loan from Pioneer for seed for the year, loaned against his asset base of 380 million. When Jaco failed to pay an installment on the loan, he was summons and a liquidation application was made simultaneously against one of his businesses, Big Creek trading. At this stage, Jaco had wheat on the land and the potential yield was estimated at 25 million Rand. Pioneer brought the liquidation application and Unigro seized the harvest. Jaco now, could not access the wheat land as the land was hired from Big Creek against which the application was lodged. If he could harvest what was ready on the land, he would have been able to pay his entire debt to Pioneer. After discussions with Nedbank, a restructuring of Jaco’s companies was on the table. Correspondence between Nedbank and Henk Strydom indicates that the bank was willing to take over the debt and restructure Jaco’s business. But, in a letter from Henk to the bank, Henk clearly states that he had orders from his client, the Land bank, to liquidate Big Creek. He was not open to any suggested rescue remedies. Meanwhile, UNIGROW instructed Jaco to harvest the wheat, although legally, that is not permitted. Jaco and his staff commenced with the harvest. As soon as Jaco moved the first load to storage, Henk brought a case of theft and contempt of court against Jaco. The paperwork started piling up and eventually Jaco would lose the fight because he could not afford the legal costs. Over the next three years, Jaco’s entire farming operation was liquidated for less than 40% of his total asset value. His asset value was 380 million and his overall debt of all his businesses combined, amounted to just under 180 million Rand. Meanwhile, Cois, who was still fighting to keep his assets, continued to try and find avenues to save what he had left. Out of frustration, he took to Facebook and publicized what he deemed to be unethical practice by Henk Strydom. Immediately, Henk hit back with a defamation case against Cois. Cois was instructed not to say anything on social media and was not allowed to mention Henk’s name. At the time, Cois had an operation on his back and was bedridden…A good place to contemplate what had happened to him. He made another post on Facebook but not mentioning Henk’s name. It was met with hundreds of replies from people who had experienced the same fate at the hands of Henk Strydom. After the follow up post was made, a police squad surrounded Cois’s home accompanied by two lawyers from Henk’s office in Pretoria. Cois was arrested and thrown in jail. Back in Thabazimbi, it was a normal working day for employees at the Koedoeskop service station and restaurant. Another business belonging to Jaco but unrelated to Big Creek. Suddenly, Henk Strydom arrived on the premises, accompanied by a security firm. He ordered all employees to seize what they were doing and closed the shop and filling station. Restaurant patrons were told to leave the premises and employees ordered to cash up and leave. The business was shutting down. In 17 affidavits, employees echo the fear and anxiety they felt that day. Later that same day, there was a break-in at the premises and all CCTV cameras were stolen. A day later, they were returned by the same security team that accompanied Henk the previous day. All visual material had been deleted. This conduct seems to be a pattern. Photos have now emerged of Henk and his friends, hunting on farms he was busy liquidating. The Land bank terminated its service level agreement with UNIGRO in October 2021. An insider source within the Land bank cited the decision taken by the board to end the agreement, based on various discrepancies. In a letter to their clients, dated October 2021, UNIGRO announced that the service level agreement between themselves and the bank was heading to an end. In the same letter, the cooperative confirms that the termination talks already started in March 2020. UNIGRO clients were advised to pay their Land bank debt straight to the Land bank. Another insider source within Henk’s personal circle told us, when Land Bank announced the termination of the SLA, Henk immediately applied for more than 40 liquidations in one go. Some of them are still ongoing. The bank and Unigro should reveal this. How many liquidation applications were brought between March 2020 and October 2021? More than 60 farmers have the same story to tell; Of a systemic operation within the legal fraternity involved. Connected between Henk Strydom, UNIGRO lawyer, Ernst Janse van Rensburg, the same set of liquidators, the same auctioneers, and a possible connection inside the Land Bank. I am in the process of getting my hands on documentation that may reveal fake creditors that were listed when payouts were made after liquidations concluded. Up to date, no copy has been seen of Land Bank’s mandate to Henk Strydom. I would also like to see the correspondence in which the Land Bank refused Nedbank’s solution to save Jaco du Toit’s Big Creek. The only documentation we have seen, is a power of attorney, given directly to Henk by Stephen Seboeng, Land Bank head of legal. Seboeng joined the bank in 2018. (The first liquidations started in 2018). According to the Land bank insider, a legal panel of the bank jointly decides on a consultant if and when the bank intends to liquidate a debtor. There was seemingly never any decision taken by the bank to mandate Henk to act as liquidator. The only said power of attorney was granted in the Mafikeng high court between Stephan and Henk. Does the Land Bank have a paper trail reflecting this and how the decision was made to mandate Henk? To add insult to injury, the only existing power of attorney is dated October 2022. Other documentation reflecting Unigro’s mandate to take legal action against debtors, is a power of attorney signed by a regional manager of the Land Bank and four financial agents of Unigro: Ernst Janse van Rensburg is one of them. We know that Ernst and Henk are friends, golf and hunting buddies- but unfortunately, I cannot prove that, except to ask them. Unigro is protecting Ernst. I also know that Ernst was looking for another job mid last year, but I cannot prove that either. The question remains, did the Land bank ever mandate Henk Strydom to liquidate farmers? In the long-term interest of national food security, was the bank aware that farmers were forced off their land and that this resulted in a general perception that the bank wanted white farmers off the land? Is there any truth in that? Liquidation should be the last resort when debt collection fails, according to industry experts. Should the farmers not have been offered restructuring? business rescue? How is it possible that the bank could give Strydom an order to liquidate Jaco’s Big Creek, if Nedbank was willing to take over the debt? Cois Harman has lost everything. He should be entering into rehabilitation now that the liquidation and sequestration have concluded. But the defamation suits continue, and Henk slammed Cois with a legal bill of 1.3 million Rand in October 2021. According to Cois’s lawyers, Henk is now targeting Cois’s son to recover the money. Meanwhile, du Toit, the once commercial farmer, who created employment for over 600 people, are now living in a garden cottage of someone’s backyard. He had lost all he had left because the legal fees that came from Henk’s office never stopped.
